resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of intensive conservative therapy.
New or worsening neurological deficits at any point during the conservative trial.
Progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or contrast enhancement on follow-up cervical MRI at 3 months.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with subacute progressive cervical myelopathy, severe spastic quadriparesis, and sphincter dysfunction. Imaging shows two-level spondylotic cord compression with extensive intramedullary T2 signal, cord enlargement, and contrast enhancement. The enhancement and cord enlargement are not typical for pure spondylotic myelopathy and raise concern for an intrinsic cord lesion (neoplasm, demyelinating, inflammatory, vascular) either as the primary pathology or superimposed on compression. Given the progressive and severe neurological deficits, I consider conservative management unsafe; a 3–6 month trial risks irreversible loss. However, proceeding to decompression alone without tissue diagnosis may fail to treat an underlying intrinsic process. Therefore, I favor urgent surgical intervention that combines decompression with biopsy of the enhancing region, with the approach guided by review of the actual MRI and any additional imaging.
proposed_options: Urgent posterior cervical laminectomy/laminoplasty with intraoperative ultrasound and biopsy of enhancing intramedullary lesion, plus decompression of stenosis (if posterior elements contribute; if anterior compression predominates, consider adding anterior approach later or staged).
Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C5-6 and C6-7, with separate or delayed posterior open biopsy of cord lesion if needed.

Expedited nonoperative diagnostic workup (contrast MRI with axial/sagittal detailed, CSF analysis for oligoclonal bands, NMO/AQP4, cytology, serum inflammatory markers, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for primary) followed by targeted surgery, but only if can be completed within days, not months; while awaiting, consider high-dose steroids if inflammatory suspected but only under neurology guidance.

Emergent surgical decompression only, without biopsy, accepting risk of missing intrinsic lesion, reserved for acute deterioration with life/function-threatening compression where biopsy not feasible.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent surgical decompression (posterior approach preferred to access the cord lesion) with intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion, after expedited additional imaging and CSF studies if they can be done without meaningful delay.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3–6 month conservative trial; severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction is a surgical emergency and delay risks permanent neurological injury.

I disagree with treating this as straightforward cervical spondylotic myelopathy: intramedullary enhancement and cord enlargement are red flags for intrinsic pathology, so decompression alone may be inadequate and could leave a tumor or inflammatory lesion untreated.

I disagree that an anterior-only decompression is sufficient without addressing the enhancing lesion; at minimum, we need intraoperative biopsy or a separate posterior procedure, and the choice must be based on the actual MRI, which I have not yet reviewed.

I disagree with proceeding to open biopsy without concurrent decompression in a patient with severe cord compression and myelopathy, as laminectomy alone to expose the cord may not relieve anterior compression and could worsen instability.

If biopsy shows inflammatory/demyelinating pathology, who will coordinate medical management afterward? Should we involve neurology/neuroimmunology preoperatively?
What is your preference for the extent of decompression: address both C5-6 and C6-7, or only the more severe level?

vice_opinions.assessment: This is an urgent surgical case: progressive severe myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and an enhancing intramedullary lesion at C5-C6. The dominant issue is not just spondylotic compression; tissue diagnosis is essential because inflammatory, demyelinating, or neoplastic pathology could respond to medical therapy, and decompression alone risks leaving a treatable process untreated. Surgical decompression plus biopsy should proceed without delay; parallel CSF/serum studies are appropriate only if they do not delay the OR beyond 48 hours. Final approach must be based on personal review of the MRI, with attention to the predominant compression vector, cord expansion, and the location of the enhancing lesion relative to the dorsal midline sulcus.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical decompression (laminectomy with or without instrumented fusion) plus midline myelotomy and biopsy of the enhancing C5-C6 lesion; this is the safest corridor for intramedullary biopsy and can be combined with fusion to address instability, though ventral compressive pathology may require a staged anterior procedure later.

Anterior cervical decompression at C5-C6 and C6-C7 (discectomy/corpectomy with fusion) plus intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing lesion through the anterior approach only if the lesion reaches the ventral cord surface and compression is predominantly ventral.
Staged approach: urgent posterior decompression and biopsy first to obtain tissue and relieve cord tension, then reassess for anterior decompression if ventral compression remains symptomatic.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical decompression with midline myelotomy and biopsy, using intraoperative ultrasound and neurophysiological monitoring, with instrumented fusion; if review of the MRI shows dominant ventral compression with minimal dorsal cord expansion, I would consider a staged anterior decompression after tissue diagnosis.

CSF and serum studies are unlikely to be definitively diagnostic for an intramedullary mass and must not delay surgery beyond the 48-hour limit the director set.
I would not attempt biopsy through an anterior approach if the enhancing lesion is dorsal or central, as this adds risk without benefit; the posterior midline sulcus is the safer route.
